title: A chart of who looks at whom
allegory: An attention pattern is the glance chart of a dinner party where guests arrive in order: each guest has exactly one unit of attention to split among the guests already seated, and the chart records who looked at whom and how much.
map: each guest's one unit of attention, split among others
one row of the pattern: a softmax over keys that sums to 1
you can only look at guests already seated
the causal mask: the pattern is lower-triangular
the glance chart: who looks at whom, how much
pattern[query, key] for one head on one prompt
a habit you can name from the chart

chapters.name: What does it do?
chapters.note: so many heads. which one does what?

cap.1: A transformer has many attention heads, each a small block of numbers. You want to know what one of them does. Where do you even start?
cap.2: A head's weights are opaque matrices. The cheapest first look: run a prompt, pull that head's attention pattern from the cache, and see where each token looks.
cap.3: Weights alone rarely reveal function. The attention pattern, post-softmax, per head, per prompt, is the first observable: which source positions each destination reads.

cap.1: Picture guests arriving at a dinner one by one. Each has exactly one unit of attention to split among the guests already seated. Who glances at whom?
cap.2: For each token (the query), a head splits 100% of its attention across earlier tokens (the keys) and itself. Write those splits down for every token and you have the pattern.
cap.3: pattern[q, k] = softmax over k of q·k/√d_head, with the causal mask applied: a row-stochastic, lower-triangular matrix per head, specific to this prompt.

chapters.name: The glance chart
chapters.title: rows = who is looking, columns = who is looked at

cap.1: As a chart: one row per guest doing the looking, one column per guest looked at. This head's habit is to look at the guest just before you.
cap.2: Rows are queries (destination), columns are keys (source). Every row sums to 1, the top-right is all 0, and the mass sits just below the diagonal: a previous-token head.
cap.3: Row-stochastic and lower-triangular; mass on the (i, i−1) off-diagonal marks a previous-token head. In TransformerLens, cache['pattern', layer] is (batch, head, query, key).

parts.note: each guest's glance at the one before

cap.1: To find 'look at the guest before' heads automatically, average every guest's glance at the one just before. A high average names the habit.
cap.2: Each detector is a one-liner: the mean of the diagonal (current-token), of the diagonal just below it (previous-token), or of column 0 (first-token), then a threshold.
cap.3: Shape scores: mean diag(P) for current-token, mean diag(P, −1) for previous-token, mean P[:, 0] for first-token. Threshold, and average over several prompts, not one.

chapters.name: Looks, not does

right.title: what it does not show
lines: what gets passed along (the OV side)

chapters.verdict: Name the shape first, then test it.

cap.1: The chart shows who glances at whom, not what gets whispered or whether it changes the conversation. It is a first clue, not a verdict.
cap.2: A pattern shows where a head reads, not what it writes (the OV circuit) or whether it matters (ablate or patch it). And read along rows: rows sum to 1, columns do not.
cap.3: Patterns are prompt-specific and silent on the OV map and on causal effect. Practice: eyeball, name the shape, score it, then confirm with ablation or patching before claiming a role.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: The first picture of any head
Induction heads show up as a stripe

cap.1: Heads you will meet later, like induction heads, have tell-tale shapes in charts like this. Looking comes first; proof comes after.
cap.2: In [1.2] you plot patterns with circuitsvis, then write detectors for current-, previous- and first-token heads. Naming the shape before scoring it is the real research habit.
cap.3: To understand and steer a model you first locate mechanism: patterns show where information flows, so you know which heads to ablate, patch or steer through.

coda.title: Paint a head: tap to add glances (row = looker, column = looked at)

readouts.label: current-token score
readouts.f: mean(G.map((row, i) => [row.map((v, j) => j <= i ? v : 0)].map(m => sum(m) > 0 ? m.map(v => v / sum(m)) : m.map((v, j) => j <= i ? 1/(i + 1) : 0))[0]).slice(1).map((row, k) => row[k + 1])).toFixed(2)

readouts.label: previous-token score
readouts.f: mean(G.map((row, i) => [row.map((v, j) => j <= i ? v : 0)].map(m => sum(m) > 0 ? m.map(v => v / sum(m)) : m.map((v, j) => j <= i ? 1/(i + 1) : 0))[0]).slice(1).map((row, k) => row[k])).toFixed(2)

readouts.label: first-token score
readouts.f: mean(G.map((row, i) => [row.map((v, j) => j <= i ? v : 0)].map(m => sum(m) > 0 ? m.map(v => v / sum(m)) : m.map((v, j) => j <= i ? 1/(i + 1) : 0))[0]).slice(1).map(row => row[0])).toFixed(2)

readouts.label: verdict
readouts.f: [G.map((row, i) => [row.map((v, j) => j <= i ? v : 0)].map(m => sum(m) > 0 ? m.map(v => v / sum(m)) : m.map((v, j) => j <= i ? 1/(i + 1) : 0))[0]).slice(1)].map(P => [mean(P.map((row, k) => row[k + 1])), mean(P.map((row, k) => row[k])), mean(P.map(row => row[0]))]).map(s => max(...s) < 0.5 ? 'no clear habit: a mixed head' : ['a current-token head', 'a previous-token head', 'a first-token head'][s.indexOf(max(...s))])[0]

readouts.label: taps above the diagonal (blocked by the causal mask)
readouts.f: sum(G.map((row, i) => sum(row.filter((v, j) => j > i))))

caption.1: Paint a head's habits: tap cells to add glances, and each row is shared out to sum to 1. Try the diagonal, the cells just below it, or the first column.
caption.2: Taps become weights; each row is masked (no looking ahead) and normalised, like a real pattern. The readouts are the three [1.2] detectors: current, previous and first-token.
caption.3: Rows are masked then normalised; an empty row becomes uniform, as softmax of equal scores would. Scores average diag, diag(−1) and column 0 over rows 1 to 4 (row 0 is forced).

where_else: Markov chains: a row-stochastic transition matrix, each row a split of probability
Cross-attention in translation and image-generation models: the same chart, with queries and keys from different sequences
Later circuits such as induction heads: first recognised by the shape of their pattern

hamming.what: A head's matrix of attention weights, showing for each token how it splits its attention over earlier tokens.
hamming.when: The first thing you look at when asking what a head does, from [1.2] onwards in every circuit hunt.
hamming.why: It is the cheapest direct window into where information flows, which tells you which heads are worth testing properly.

object.title: The glance landscape
object.subtitle: One head's pattern on 'A B C A B C' as a landscape of towers; switch the habit and blur it.

knobs.label: how spread out the glances are

cap.1: Each row is one token looking back; tower height is how much it looks. This head always looks at itself: a ridge down the diagonal.
cap.2: A current-token head: all mass on the diagonal. The flat top-right is the causal mask at work.
cap.3: Idealised current-token head: P = I. Height = 1.6·P + 0.03 so masked cells stay visible as a floor.

cap.1: Switch habit: now every token looks at the one just before it. The ridge slides one step off the diagonal.
cap.2: A previous-token head: mass on the sub-diagonal. Row 0 has nowhere else to look, so it looks at itself.
cap.3: P[i, i−1] = 1 for i ≥ 1; the first row is forced to P[0, 0] = 1 by the mask plus normalisation.

cap.1: Now everyone looks at the very first token: a wall along the first column. Researchers often read this as a head with nothing better to do.
cap.2: A first-token head: every row puts its mass on position 0, often interpreted as the head resting.
cap.3: P[:, 0] = 1: a first-token head, commonly read as a default or null position when nothing relevant is present.

cap.1: On repeated text, an induction head looks at the token right after the last time the current token appeared. A stripe appears in the second half.
cap.2: At the second A, it looks at the B that followed the first A: a stripe two steps below the diagonal on this 3-token repeat.
cap.3: Idealised induction pattern on period-3 repeats: P[i, i−2] for i ≥ 3, offset −(period − 1); first-token fallback before the repeat.

cap.1: Real heads are blurrier. Most attention goes to the habit and some spreads around, but every row still adds up to one.
cap.2: Blur mixes the habit with an even spread over allowed positions. Rows still sum to 1; detectors just score lower.
cap.3: P = (1 − b)·P_habit + b·U_causal, still row-stochastic. Thresholded detectors degrade gracefully as b grows.

predict.q: In an attention pattern, what always sums to 1?
predict.why: Softmax runs over the keys for each query, so every row is a distribution. Columns can sum to anything.

predict.q: Why is the top-right triangle of a GPT-style pattern always zero?

options.t: The causal mask stops tokens looking ahead

predict.why: Scores above the diagonal are set to minus infinity before the softmax, so they get zero weight.

predict.q: A head puts most of its attention on the previous token. What have you shown?

options.t: Where it reads from on these prompts: a hypothesis to test
What it writes, and that the model needs it

predict.why: Patterns show where information is read. What moves is the OV circuit; whether it matters needs ablation or patching.
